questions.title: SQL Warehouse Type for Unpredictable Concurrency
questions.question: A team has 50 analysts who run queries at unpredictable times, with sudden bursts of activity. Which SQL warehouse type best handles this workload?

choices.A: Serverless warehouse, because it starts in seconds and uses Intelligent Workload Management to scale
choices.B: Classic warehouse, because it is the lowest-cost option
choices.C: Pro warehouse, because it adds clusters after queries have queued for several minutes
choices.D: An all-purpose cluster for each analyst

questions.shortAnswer: Serverless SQL warehouses start in about 2–6 seconds and use Intelligent Workload Management (IWM) to start queries immediately when capacity exists and to add clusters quickly when queues grow.
questions.explanation: Pro and classic warehouses also autoscale, but they add clusters based on the estimated load and take about 4 minutes to start, so they respond more slowly to bursts. Per-analyst clusters are not SQL warehouses and waste compute.

questions.title: Serverless vs Pro Warehouse — Start Time
questions.question: A product team needs a SQL warehouse that is ready within seconds when the first dashboard query of the morning arrives. Which type should they choose?

choices.D: Any type — all warehouse types start in seconds

questions.shortAnswer: Serverless warehouses typically start in 2–6 seconds because Databricks manages the compute.
questions.explanation: Pro and classic warehouses typically take about 4 minutes to start (D).

questions.title: Serverless Auto Stop Default
questions.question: A workspace admin creates a serverless SQL warehouse in the UI and leaves **Auto stop** at its default value. After how many idle minutes does the warehouse stop?
questions.shortAnswer: For serverless warehouses the default auto stop is 10 minutes, and the UI minimum is 5 minutes.
questions.explanation: Pro and classic warehouses default to 45 minutes, with a 10-minute minimum. 120 minutes is not a current default. Auto stop only starts counting once no queries are running.

questions.title: Warehouse Queues at Peak
questions.question: A pro SQL warehouse is configured with **Scaling** set to a minimum and maximum of 1 cluster. During peak hours, queries wait in the queue even though each query finishes quickly once it starts. Which change addresses this?

choices.A: Increase the warehouse size from Small to Large
choices.B: Turn off the query result cache
choices.C: Raise the maximum number of clusters so the warehouse can add clusters under load

questions.shortAnswer: Scaling sets the minimum and maximum number of clusters. More clusters let the warehouse run more queries at the same time. Databricks recommends about one cluster for every 10 concurrent queries.
questions.explanation: A larger size reduces the latency of each query but does not add concurrency (A). Turning off the cache only adds work (B). Classic offers no concurrency advantage over pro (D).

questions.title: Serverless-Only Capability
questions.question: Which capability does a serverless SQL warehouse have that pro and classic warehouses do NOT have?
questions.shortAnswer: Intelligent Workload Management (IWM) is available only on serverless warehouses.
questions.explanation: Photon runs on all three types (A). Predictive I/O runs on pro and serverless (B). Auto stop is available on every type (C).

questions.title: Default Warehouse Type  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: In a workspace that supports serverless compute, an analyst creates a SQL warehouse in the UI and does not change the type. What type is created?

choices.C: The type of the most recently used warehouse

questions.shortAnswer: In the UI, the default SQL warehouse type is serverless for eligible workspaces.
questions.explanation: Through the API with default parameters, the default is classic. That difference is a common trap.

questions.title: Warehouse Size Selection
questions.question: An analyst runs complex aggregate queries over 500 GB of Delta Lake data every day. Which warehouse size is most appropriate?

choices.A: Large or X-Large, because complex queries over large data benefit from more workers
choices.C: Small, because it is designed for individual users
choices.D: Size doesn't matter, because every size returns the same result just as fast

questions.shortAnswer: Each larger size doubles the number of workers. Increasing the size reduces the latency of heavy queries.
questions.explanation: The smallest sizes suit light, exploratory work. All sizes return the same result, but not in the same time (D).

questions.title: CREATE TABLE in Unity Catalog
questions.question: Which statement creates a managed table named `transactions` in the `gold` schema of the `ml_catalog` catalog?

choices.A: `CREATE TABLE gold.transactions AS SELECT ...` with no catalog set
choices.C: `USE CATALOG ml_catalog; CREATE TABLE gold.transactions AS SELECT ...`

questions.shortAnswer: A fully qualified three-level name (B) and a `USE CATALOG` statement followed by a two-level name (C) both create the table in `ml_catalog.gold`.
questions.explanation: Without a catalog set (A), the two-level name resolves against the current default catalog, which may not be `ml_catalog`.

questions.title: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN
questions.question: A query must return all employees and their department names, including employees who have no department. Which join type should be used?

choices.A: LEFT JOIN from employees to departments

questions.shortAnswer: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table (employees). Employees without a department get NULL in the department columns.
questions.explanation: An INNER JOIN drops employees without a match. A CROSS JOIN returns every combination. A SEMI JOIN returns only matching left rows and no right-side columns.

questions.title: Joining on a Composite Key  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: The `order_lines` and `shipments` tables are both identified by `order_id` and `line_number`. An analyst joins them with `ON o.order_id = s.order_id` and sees far more rows than expected. What is the fix?

choices.A: Replace the INNER JOIN with a FULL OUTER JOIN
choices.C: Join on both keys: `ON o.order_id = s.order_id AND o.line_number = s.line_number`

questions.shortAnswer: When the key has two columns, joining on only one of them matches every line of an order to every shipment of that order, which multiplies rows.
questions.explanation: A full outer join adds even more rows (A). `DISTINCT` can hide the symptom but still pairs the wrong lines (B). Sorting does not change which rows match (D).

questions.title: Anti Join
questions.question: A query must return all customers who have NOT made a purchase. Which approaches work?

choices.A: `customers LEFT JOIN purchases ... WHERE purchases.purchase_id IS NULL`
choices.D: `customers FULL OUTER JOIN purchases ... WHERE purchases.purchase_id IS NOT NULL`

questions.shortAnswer: `LEFT ANTI JOIN` returns only left rows that have no match. A `LEFT JOIN` filtered to rows where the right key `IS NULL` produces the same result.
questions.explanation: Option D keeps rows that do have purchases, which is the opposite of what is needed.

questions.title: Semi Join
questions.question: A query must return each product that has at least one review, once per product. Which join is most appropriate?
questions.shortAnswer: A `LEFT SEMI JOIN` returns left rows where a match exists and never duplicates them.
questions.explanation: An INNER JOIN returns one row per matching review, so products with many reviews appear many times. A LEFT JOIN also keeps products with no reviews.

questions.title: UNION vs UNION ALL  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: Table `a` contains the values 1, 2, 2 and table `b` contains 2, 3. What does `SELECT x FROM a UNION SELECT x FROM b` return?
questions.shortAnswer: `UNION` defaults to `DISTINCT`, so duplicate rows are removed and the result is 1, 2, 3.
questions.explanation: `UNION ALL` keeps duplicates and would return 1, 2, 2, 2, 3 (A). Option B is what `INTERSECT` returns. Option D is what `EXCEPT` returns.

questions.title: Customers Lost Between Years  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst needs the customer IDs that bought in 2024 but not in 2025. Which query returns them?

choices.A: `SELECT customer_id FROM sales_2024 UNION SELECT customer_id FROM sales_2025`
choices.B: `SELECT customer_id FROM sales_2024 INTERSECT SELECT customer_id FROM sales_2025`
choices.C: `SELECT customer_id FROM sales_2024 EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM sales_2025`
choices.D: `SELECT customer_id FROM sales_2024 UNION ALL SELECT customer_id FROM sales_2025`

questions.shortAnswer: `EXCEPT` returns the rows of the first query that do not appear in the second. Databricks SQL also accepts `MINUS` as a synonym.
questions.explanation: `INTERSECT` returns customers who bought in both years (B). `UNION` and `UNION ALL` combine both lists (A, D). Every set operation needs the same number of columns on both sides.

questions.title: Approximate Distinct Count  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A dashboard tile shows the number of distinct visitors over billions of page views. An estimate within a few percent is acceptable if it is faster. Which function fits?
questions.shortAnswer: `approx_count_distinct` returns an estimated distinct count as a `BIGINT`. It uses the HyperLogLog++ algorithm and is accurate within 5 % by default. An optional `relativeSD` argument sets the allowed error.
questions.explanation: `count(DISTINCT ...)` is exact but more expensive (A). `count(col)` counts non-NULL values, not distinct ones (C). Option D adds up distinct IDs, which is meaningless (D).

questions.title: Summary Statistics in a Notebook  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst wants to see summary statistics for every column of a DataFrame from Python code in a notebook. Which command does this?
questions.shortAnswer: `dbutils.data.summarize` calculates and displays summary statistics for a Spark or pandas DataFrame. In the notebook UI, the data profile on a result table gives the same kind of view, including histograms. Some statistics are approximate unless you pass `precise=True`.
questions.explanation: `printSchema` shows only column names and types (B). `DESCRIBE HISTORY` lists table versions (C). `count()` returns only the row count (D).

questions.title: Window Function — ROW_NUMBER
questions.question: A query must return exactly one row per customer: the purchase with the highest amount. Which window function guarantees a unique number per row within each customer?

choices.A: `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC)`
choices.B: `DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC)`
choices.C: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC)`
choices.D: `NTILE(1) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC)`

questions.shortAnswer: `ROW_NUMBER()` numbers rows 1, 2, 3… with no ties, so filtering on `= 1` returns exactly one row per customer.
questions.explanation: `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()` give tied rows the same number, so `= 1` can return several rows. `NTILE(1)` puts every row in bucket 1.

questions.title: RANK vs DENSE_RANK
questions.question: Sales figures are Alice = 100, Bob = 100, and Carol = 90, ordered by sales descending. What are Carol's values from `RANK()` and `DENSE_RANK()`?
questions.shortAnswer: Alice and Bob tie at 1 in both functions. `RANK()` leaves a gap after a tie, so Carol is 3. `DENSE_RANK()` leaves no gaps, so Carol is 2.

questions.title: LAG Function
questions.question: A query calculates the change in monthly sales compared with the previous month. Which expression returns the previous month's value?
questions.shortAnswer: `LAG(column, offset)` returns the value from `offset` rows before the current row.
questions.explanation: `LEAD` looks forward, not backward (C). `FIRST_VALUE` returns the first value in the window, not the previous one (D). `PREV` is not a Databricks SQL function (A).

questions.title: Running Total
questions.question: An analyst needs a running total of sales by date within each region. Which expression computes it?

choices.C: `CUMSUM(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY sale_date)`
choices.D: `SUM(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY sale_date)`

questions.shortAnswer: Adding `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` makes the window grow row by row, which produces a cumulative sum within each region.
questions.explanation: Without `ORDER BY`, every row gets the partition's total (A). `GROUP BY` returns one total per region and date, not a running total (B). `CUMSUM` is not a Databricks SQL function (C).

questions.title: CTE vs Subquery
questions.question: Which statement about common table expressions (CTEs) is TRUE?

choices.A: CTEs are always faster than equivalent subqueries
choices.B: CTEs name an intermediate result, which improves readability, and the name can be referenced more than once in the query
choices.C: CTEs cannot be used in `SELECT` statements
choices.D: CTEs are stored as tables after the query finishes

questions.shortAnswer: A CTE (`WITH name AS (...)`) names an intermediate result for the duration of one statement. You can reference it several times without repeating the logic.
questions.explanation: CTEs are a readability tool, not a guaranteed speed-up (A), and nothing is persisted after the statement ends (D).

questions.title: One Row per Array Element
questions.question: A table has a `tags` column of type `ARRAY<STRING>`. A query needs one output row per tag. Which function produces this?
questions.shortAnswer: `EXPLODE` is a generator function that returns one row per array element.
questions.explanation: `FLATTEN` merges nested arrays into one array without adding rows (A). `ARRAY_JOIN` concatenates the elements into a single string (B). `SPLIT` turns a string into an array, which is the opposite direction (C).

questions.title: Aggregating Values into an Array
questions.question: Which aggregate function collects the values of many rows into one array per group?
questions.shortAnswer: `COLLECT_LIST` returns an array of the group's values. `ARRAY_AGG` is the SQL-standard name for the same aggregate.
questions.explanation: `CONCAT_WS` joins strings with a separator but is not an aggregate (B). `EXPLODE` does the reverse, turning one array into many rows (C).

questions.title: Pivoting Months into Columns
questions.question: An analyst wants monthly sales as columns (Jan, Feb, Mar), one row per product. Which clause does this most concisely?

choices.B: `CASE WHEN month = 'Jan' THEN sales END` in the `SELECT` list, with no aggregation

questions.shortAnswer: `PIVOT` turns the distinct values of one column into columns and aggregates a measure for each: `FROM t PIVOT (agg(col) FOR pivot_col IN (values))`.
questions.explanation: Conditional aggregation can produce the same shape, but only with `SUM(CASE ...)` and `GROUP BY product`. Without aggregation, option B returns one row per input row. Option C keeps the months as rows, and `TRANSPOSE` is not a Databricks SQL function.

questions.title: Days Between Two Dates
questions.question: Which expression returns the number of days from `order_date` to today as a positive number for past orders?
questions.shortAnswer: `datediff(endDate, startDate)` returns the number of days from `startDate` to `endDate` as an `INTEGER`. The end date comes first.
questions.explanation: Swapping the arguments returns a negative number for past orders (A). `months_between` measures months (C). `date_sub` subtracts a number of days from a date and returns a date (D).

questions.title: Sorting with NULLs  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst runs `SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY price ASC`. Some prices are NULL. Where do those rows appear, and how can the analyst move them to the end?

choices.A: Last by default; nothing to change
choices.B: They are excluded from sorted results; add `WHERE price IS NULL`

questions.shortAnswer: In Databricks SQL, NULLs sort first for `ASC` and last for `DESC` unless you say otherwise. `ORDER BY price ASC NULLS LAST` keeps ascending order and moves NULLs to the end.
questions.explanation: Sorting never removes rows (B). Switching to `DESC` moves the NULLs but reverses the order of the prices (D).

questions.title: Diagnosing an Error with the Assistant  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A SQL cell in a notebook fails with an error. The analyst wants Databricks Assistant to propose a corrected version of the code. Which command should they use?
questions.shortAnswer: `/fix` proposes fixes for code errors in a diff view. The **Diagnose error** button that appears under a failed cell runs `/fix` automatically.
questions.explanation: `/explain` describes what code does (A). `/doc` adds comments (B). `/findTables` searches Unity Catalog metadata for relevant tables (C). Databricks Assistant was renamed **Genie Code** on March 11, 2026, and these commands still work under the new name.

questions.title: Federated Join  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst must join a Unity Catalog Delta table `main.sales.orders` with a `customers` table that lives in an operational PostgreSQL database. Copying the PostgreSQL data is not allowed. What is the Databricks approach?

choices.A: Use Lakehouse Federation: create a connection and a foreign catalog for PostgreSQL, then join the foreign table to the Delta table using three-level names
choices.B: Load the PostgreSQL table with `COPY INTO` and then join it
choices.C: Ask the PostgreSQL team to send the data through Delta Sharing
choices.D: Export the PostgreSQL table to CSV and upload it through the UI

questions.shortAnswer: Lakehouse Federation gives governed, read-only access to external databases through Unity Catalog foreign catalogs. Queries are pushed down to the source over JDBC, so the data stays where it is. A query can join a foreign table to a Delta table like any other two tables.
questions.explanation: Options B and D copy the data. Delta Sharing (now called OpenSharing) shares data between platforms and is not a way to query a PostgreSQL database (C).

questions.title: Warehouse for Federated Queries  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A federated query against a foreign catalog fails on one SQL warehouse but works on another. Which warehouse type cannot run Lakehouse Federation queries?
questions.shortAnswer: Lakehouse Federation needs a pro or serverless SQL warehouse (version 2023.40 or above). Clusters need Databricks Runtime 13.3 LTS or above in standard or dedicated access mode.
questions.explanation: Foreign catalogs are read-only, so federated sources can be queried and joined but not written to.

questions.title: Streaming Table vs Materialized View  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: New JSON files land in a Unity Catalog volume every few minutes. An analyst wants a table that loads only the new files on each refresh. Which object fits?

choices.A: A streaming table: `CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE ... AS SELECT * FROM STREAM read_files(...)`
choices.C: A materialized view that re-reads every file on each refresh

questions.shortAnswer: A streaming table processes only the rows that arrived since the last update and appends them. With `STREAM read_files`, it uses Auto Loader to pick up new files incrementally.
questions.explanation: Materialized views fit complex queries such as aggregations and joins whose results are precomputed and refreshed (C). Standard and temporary views store nothing and re-read the source each time (B, D).

questions.title: View vs Materialized View  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: What is the key difference between a standard (or dynamic) view and a materialized view in Databricks SQL?

choices.A: A standard view runs its query every time it is read; a materialized view stores the results and updates them on refresh
choices.B: A standard view stores its results; a materialized view runs its query every time it is read
choices.C: Only materialized views can be granted to other users
choices.D: Only standard views can be used in dashboards

questions.shortAnswer: A materialized view is a Unity Catalog managed table that stores a query's results and updates them on refresh, incrementally when possible. A standard view stores only the query text. A dynamic view is a standard view that uses functions such as `is_account_group_member()` to filter rows or mask columns for each user.
questions.explanation: Both kinds can be granted (C) and used in dashboards (D).

questions.title: Refresh When the Source Changes  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst wants a materialized view to refresh automatically whenever its source table is updated, without managing a schedule. Which clause should they use?
questions.shortAnswer: `CREATE OR REPLACE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv TRIGGER ON UPDATE AS SELECT ...` refreshes the view automatically when the source table is updated.
questions.explanation: `SCHEDULE EVERY` or `SCHEDULE CRON` refreshes on a timetable (A). `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW mv ASYNC` starts one manual refresh without waiting for it (B). Option C is not valid syntax.

questions.title: Pre-computing a Slow Dashboard Query
questions.question: Every time someone opens a dashboard, the same heavy aggregation runs over a large fact table. The data changes once per night. Which approach cuts load time most while keeping the numbers current?

choices.A: Let each dashboard query run the aggregation when the dashboard opens
choices.B: Move the dashboard to a larger SQL warehouse
choices.C: Rely only on the query result cache
choices.D: Create a materialized view with the aggregation, refreshed on a nightly schedule, and point the dashboard dataset at it

questions.shortAnswer: A materialized view runs the expensive aggregation once per refresh and stores the result, so every dashboard read is a cheap scan. Scheduling the refresh after the nightly load keeps it current.
questions.explanation: A larger warehouse still repeats the heavy query for every session (B). The result cache is invalidated when the tables change and only helps identical repeated queries (C).

questions.title: Unified Table from Files and Delta  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: Customer data arrives as CSV files in a volume and product data as Parquet files. Orders are already in a Delta table. An analyst wants one managed table that joins all three. Which statement does this in SQL?

choices.A: `CREATE VIEW unified AS SELECT * FROM csv.customers, parquet.products`
choices.B: `CREATE TABLE unified AS SELECT ... FROM read_files('/Volumes/main/raw/customers', format => 'csv') c JOIN read_files('/Volumes/main/raw/products', format => 'parquet') p ON ... JOIN main.sales.orders o ON ...`
choices.D: `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE unified USING CSV, PARQUET, DELTA`

questions.shortAnswer: `read_files` reads CSV, JSON, Parquet, Avro, ORC, XML, text, and binary files as a table. Used inside `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT`, it can be joined with Delta tables to create a new managed table.
questions.explanation: `COPY INTO` loads files, not Delta tables (C). A table has one format, so option D is invalid, and option A is not valid syntax for reading files.

questions.title: Time Travel to Yesterday  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst needs the `orders` table as it was at midnight on October 25, 2026. Which query works?
questions.shortAnswer: Delta Lake time travel uses `TIMESTAMP AS OF <timestamp>` or `VERSION AS OF <version>`. You can also write `orders@v123` for a version.
questions.explanation: Use `DESCRIBE HISTORY orders` to find the version numbers and timestamps that exist. The other options are not valid syntax.

questions.title: Time Travel Fails for an Old Version  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A Delta table uses the default retention settings, and `VACUUM` runs on it every week. `DESCRIBE HISTORY` still lists a version from 20 days ago, but `SELECT ... VERSION AS OF` that version fails. Why?

choices.A: History is kept for only 7 days by default
choices.B: Time travel works only on external tables
choices.C: The table was optimized with liquid clustering
choices.D: `VACUUM` deleted the data files that the old version needs; by default it removes files that have been unreferenced for more than 7 days

questions.shortAnswer: Table history is kept for 30 days by default (`logRetentionDuration`), so the version still appears. `VACUUM` deletes unreferenced data files older than `deletedFileRetentionDuration`, which defaults to 7 days. Once those files are gone, you cannot read or restore that version.
questions.explanation: Time travel works on managed and external Delta tables (B). Clustering does not remove history (C).

questions.title: Replace a Table Safely  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst must rebuild `warehouse_db.product_inventory` with a new definition. Users already have `SELECT` on the table and rely on its history. Which approach keeps both?

choices.C: `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS warehouse_db.product_inventory (...)`

questions.shortAnswer: For Delta tables, `REPLACE` keeps the table history and the granted privileges, row filters, and column masks. Databricks strongly recommends `REPLACE` over dropping and re-creating a table.
questions.explanation: Dropping loses the history and grants (A). `IF NOT EXISTS` does nothing when the table exists (B). `OR REPLACE` and `IF NOT EXISTS` cannot be combined (C).

questions.title: Showing a Single KPI
questions.question: Which AI/BI dashboard visualization displays one aggregated number prominently, such as total revenue?
questions.shortAnswer: A counter displays a single value prominently and can compare it against an offset value, which suits KPIs.
questions.explanation: A table shows rows and columns, a line chart shows change over time, and a pivot summarises values across two dimensions.

questions.title: Legacy Dashboards
questions.question: A team still has dashboards built in the legacy Databricks SQL dashboard editor. What does Databricks recommend?

choices.A: Use AI/BI dashboards; legacy dashboards are no longer supported and new ones cannot be created
choices.B: Keep building new legacy dashboards because they run queries faster
choices.C: Export legacy dashboards to PDF and stop using dashboards

questions.shortAnswer: AI/BI dashboards (previously called Lakeview dashboards) are the current dashboarding product. Databricks has retired the legacy dashboard documentation, you can no longer create legacy dashboards, and Databricks recommends AI/BI dashboards instead.
questions.explanation: Dashboard speed depends on the queries and the warehouse, not the editor (B).

questions.title: Daily Dashboard Refresh
questions.question: A stakeholder needs a dashboard to refresh automatically every morning at 8 AM. How should this be configured?

choices.A: Click **Schedule** on the dashboard and set the frequency, time, and time zone
choices.B: Do nothing, because dashboards refresh only when opened
choices.C: Write a notebook that screenshots the dashboard and schedule it as a job
choices.D: Dashboards cannot be scheduled, so schedule each query instead

questions.shortAnswer: The **Schedule** button on an AI/BI dashboard sets the frequency, start time, and time zone, with optional cron syntax. By default the scheduled run uses the dashboard's SQL warehouse, and you can choose another one in the advanced settings.
questions.explanation: Schedules can also send snapshots to subscribers, so no custom notebook is needed (C).

questions.title: Alert Threshold
questions.question: An analyst creates a SQL alert on a query that returns the count of failed transactions. The alert should trigger when the count is greater than 100. How should the condition be set?
questions.shortAnswer: An alert condition compares a column to a threshold using an operator. The column can be the value in the first row or an aggregate across rows, such as `SUM` or `AVG`, and the threshold is a static value by default. "Greater than 100" is `> 100`.
questions.explanation: `>=` would also trigger at exactly 100 (D). `= 100` triggers only at 100 (B), and `IS NULL` checks for missing values (A).

questions.title: Sending an Alert to Slack
questions.question: A SQL alert must post to a Slack channel when it triggers. How is this set up?

choices.A: A workspace admin creates a Slack notification destination, and the alert author selects it in the alert's notification settings
choices.B: The alert author pastes the Slack password into the alert query
choices.C: A Python script polls the alert status every minute
choices.D: Alerts can notify only by email

questions.shortAnswer: Workspace admins set up notification destinations. Alert authors then choose users or destinations in the alert's notification settings. **Notify on OK** can also send a message when the alert returns to normal.
questions.explanation: No custom polling is needed (C), and alerts are not limited to email (D).

questions.title: Sharing with Account Users
questions.question: A manager wants a published AI/BI dashboard to be viewable by partner users who are registered in the Databricks account but are not members of the workspace. What should they do?

choices.A: Add every partner to the workspace with edit rights
choices.B: Email a CSV export every week
choices.C: Share the published dashboard with those account users, or allow anyone in the account to view it
choices.D: Use Delta Sharing to share the dashboard

questions.shortAnswer: Published dashboards can be shared with account users who have no workspace access. Those users are limited to the CAN RUN permission, and they sign in with email, a one-time passcode, or SSO.
questions.explanation: Adding everyone to the workspace grants far more access than needed (A). Delta Sharing (now OpenSharing) shares data, not dashboards (D).

questions.title: Trend over Time
questions.question: Sales data must show the trend over 12 months. Which visualization is most appropriate?
questions.shortAnswer: Line charts present the change in one or more metrics over time.
questions.explanation: Bar charts suit comparisons across categories. Scatter plots show the relationship between two numeric variables. Pie charts show proportions of a whole.

questions.title: Detailed Ranked List
questions.question: Which scenario is best suited to a table visualization?

choices.A: Total revenue as one KPI number
choices.C: The top 20 products with their revenue, units sold, and rank
choices.D: The share of sales by region

questions.shortAnswer: Tables show many columns per row and let you reorder, hide, and format columns, which suits detailed lists.
questions.explanation: KPIs use counters (A), trends use line charts (B), and proportions use pie or bar charts (D).

questions.title: Alert Schedule for an SLA
questions.question: A SQL alert watches for inventory dropping below a reorder threshold. The business must be notified within one hour. What schedule is appropriate?
questions.shortAnswer: Alerts run their query on a schedule and evaluate the condition each time. An hourly (or shorter) schedule meets a one-hour notification requirement.
questions.explanation: Alerts are not evaluated on a continuous stream (C). A daily schedule misses the requirement (B), and manual evaluation is not automated (D).

questions.title: Parameter Syntax in a Dashboard Dataset
questions.question: A dashboard dataset must accept a date selected by viewers. Which syntax does the dataset query use?
questions.shortAnswer: AI/BI dashboards, the current SQL editor, notebooks, and Genie use named parameter markers: a colon followed by the parameter name.
questions.explanation: The double-brace mustache syntax (B) is legacy and works only in the legacy SQL editor. Dashboards do not support it, so queries that use it must be converted to named markers.

questions.title: Region Dropdown
questions.question: A dashboard needs a control that lets viewers pick one region from a list, and the selected region filters a dataset through the `:region` parameter. What should the author add?

choices.D: A filter widget with a single-value selector bound to the `:region` parameter

questions.shortAnswer: Parameters can be bound to filter widgets so that viewers' choices are passed into the query. A single-value selector restricts the choice to one value from a list.
questions.explanation: Text widgets display content and do not pass values (A). A counter is a visualization (C).

questions.title: Multi-Select Parameter
questions.question: A dashboard parameter `:categories` has **Allow multiple selections** turned on. Which `WHERE` clause handles one or many selected values?
questions.shortAnswer: A multi-select parameter is passed as an array, so the query must use `ARRAY_CONTAINS`. Adding `OR :categories IS NULL` handles the "All" selection.
questions.explanation: The other options compare a single value to an array. `IN ({{ ... }})` was a pattern for the legacy mustache syntax.

questions.title: Embedding for External Users
questions.question: A company wants to embed a published AI/BI dashboard in its customer portal. The customers do not have Databricks accounts. Which approach does Databricks support?

choices.A: Basic iframe embedding, which needs no sign-in
choices.C: Exporting the dashboard to HTML and hosting it
choices.D: Embedding for external users, where the application authenticates to Databricks with a service principal

questions.shortAnswer: Embedding for external users lets viewers without Databricks accounts see a dashboard. The application authenticates with a service principal and an OAuth secret, and the tokens are valid for one hour.
questions.explanation: Basic embedding requires viewers to sign in with Databricks credentials (A). Only published dashboards can be embedded, and workspace admins must define the surfaces where embedding is allowed.

questions.title: Dashboard Refresh vs Alert Evaluation
questions.question: What is the difference between a dashboard schedule and a SQL alert schedule?

choices.B: Dashboards refresh automatically, while alerts never run on a schedule
choices.C: A dashboard schedule refreshes the dashboard's data and can send snapshots; an alert schedule runs the alert query, evaluates the condition, and notifies when it is met
choices.D: Alerts can be built only on dashboard datasets

questions.shortAnswer: Dashboards and alerts are separate objects with their own schedules. An alert evaluates to OK, TRIGGERED, or ERROR each time it runs.
questions.explanation: In the latest alerts, the query is written in the alert itself, so an existing saved query cannot be reused (D).

questions.title: Pages and Datasets  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A dashboard needs an executive summary page and a detailed operations page. Each page shows charts from different tables. How is this built in AI/BI dashboards?

choices.A: Build two dashboards and link them with a URL
choices.B: Create one dataset that joins every table, because a dashboard allows only one dataset
choices.C: Add a second page to the canvas and define several datasets on the Data tab
choices.D: Use a notebook dashboard for the second page

questions.shortAnswer: New dashboards start with one page, and you add more with the plus icon next to the page title. The Data tab holds the dashboard's datasets, defined from tables, views, or custom SQL. Visualizations on any page can use any dataset.
questions.explanation: A dashboard is not limited to one dataset (B).

questions.title: Text and Images  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An author wants a short explanation and the company logo at the top of a dashboard. Which widget types are used?

choices.B: A text widget for the explanation and an image widget for the logo
choices.D: Images are not supported in dashboards

questions.shortAnswer: AI/BI dashboards support visualization, filter, text, and image widgets.
questions.explanation: Widget titles and descriptions also support rich text formatting.

questions.title: Chart from a Query Result  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst runs a query in the SQL editor and wants a bar chart of the result. What is the quickest way?

choices.A: Click **+** above the result, select **Visualization**, and choose the type
choices.B: Export the result to CSV and build the chart elsewhere
choices.C: Create a dashboard first, because visualizations exist only on dashboards

questions.shortAnswer: In both the SQL editor and notebooks, you click **+** above a result and select **Visualization** to open the visualization editor.
questions.explanation: In a notebook, a visualization from a SQL cell can also be added to a dashboard. Visualizations from non-SQL cells and data profiles can be added only to a notebook dashboard.

questions.title: Testing a Dataset Parameter  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An author adds `WHERE region = :region` to a dashboard dataset and wants to check the query before publishing. How is the parameter tested?

choices.A: Publish the dashboard and ask a viewer to try it
choices.B: Replace `:region` with a literal, run it, then put the marker back
choices.C: Type a value in the field under the parameter name in the dataset editor and run the query
choices.D: Parameters cannot be tested in the dataset editor

questions.shortAnswer: To test, type a value into the text field under the parameter name and run the query. Running it also saves that value as the parameter's default.
questions.explanation: No publishing or query editing is needed (A, B).

questions.title: Date Range Parameter  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A dashboard parameter `:ship_date` is a date range. Which clause filters the dataset to the selected range?
questions.shortAnswer: A date range parameter exposes `.min` and `.max` values. Adding `OR :ship_date IS NULL` handles the "All" selection.
questions.explanation: `.start` and `.end` are not the property names (A). Option B is legacy mustache syntax, which dashboards do not support.

questions.title: Publishing with Viewer Permissions  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A sales table has a Unity Catalog row filter so each rep sees only their own region. After a dashboard is published, every rep sees all regions. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?

choices.A: Row filters do not apply to dashboards, so add a dashboard filter
choices.B: The warehouse is too small, so increase its size
choices.C: The row filter must be attached to the dashboard instead of the table
choices.D: The dashboard was published with shared data permissions, so queries run with the publisher's credentials; republish with individual data permissions

questions.shortAnswer: By default, viewers run queries with the publisher's credentials (shared data permissions), so the row filter evaluates the publisher's identity. With individual data permissions, viewers run queries with their own credentials, and the row filter applies per viewer.
questions.explanation: Row filters are attached to tables and apply to every query (A, C). Warehouse size has nothing to do with access (B).

questions.title: Snapshot to a Teams Channel  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team wants a snapshot of a dashboard posted to a Microsoft Teams channel every Monday at 9 AM. What should the dashboard author do?

choices.A: Share the dashboard link in Teams once
choices.B: Create a SQL alert with a condition that is always true
choices.D: Create a schedule for Monday 9 AM and add a Teams notification destination as a subscriber

questions.shortAnswer: Schedules can have subscribers, including Slack and Microsoft Teams notification destinations that a workspace admin has configured. Teams and Slack subscribers receive a PNG snapshot, a link to the dashboard, and a PDF. Email subscribers receive a PDF snapshot.
questions.explanation: A subscription list can hold up to 100 subscribers, and a notification destination counts as one.

questions.title: Relationship Between Two Measures  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst wants to show whether advertising spend and revenue move together across 200 campaigns. Which visualization communicates this best?
questions.shortAnswer: Scatter plots show the relationship between two numeric variables. Each campaign is one point.
questions.explanation: Pie charts show proportions (A), counters show one value (B), and funnels show drop-off between stages (D).

questions.title: Filter or Parameter?  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A dashboard over a large dataset needs a region selector, plus a city selector that shows only cities in the chosen region. What does Databricks recommend considering first?

choices.A: Field filters, which support cascading and often perform better on large datasets
choices.B: A parameter in every dataset query
choices.D: A text widget listing the regions

questions.shortAnswer: Field filters filter a dataset's fields, support cascading behaviour, and often perform better on large datasets, so Databricks recommends considering them first.
questions.explanation: Parameters change the query itself. They are useful when the value must go inside the SQL, for example in a calculation or a function argument.

questions.title: Diagnosing a Slow Query
questions.question: A query in Databricks SQL runs slower than expected. Which feature helps the analyst diagnose it?

choices.D: Query history, which shows the query's duration, rows, and I/O, with a link to its query profile

questions.shortAnswer: Query history lists each query with its status, duration, rows returned, and I/O details. **See query profile** opens the execution plan with metrics for each operator.
questions.explanation: MLflow tracks ML experiments (A), and the Delta log records table changes, not query performance (C).

questions.title: Filtering on a Window Function
questions.question: An analyst wants only the top product by revenue in each category. Which clause filters on a window function result without a subquery?

choices.B: `WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) = 1`
choices.C: `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) = 1`

questions.shortAnswer: `QUALIFY` filters on window function results, just as `HAVING` filters on aggregates.
questions.explanation: `WHERE` is evaluated before window functions, so it cannot reference them (B). `HAVING` filters groups after `GROUP BY` (A). `FILTER (WHERE ...)` applies to an aggregate's input rows (D).

questions.title: Aggregate in WHERE
questions.question: An analyst writes `SELECT region, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 GROUP BY region` and gets an error. What fixes the query?

choices.B: Move the condition to `HAVING COUNT(*) > 5` after `GROUP BY`

questions.shortAnswer: `WHERE` filters rows before aggregation, so it cannot contain aggregate functions. `HAVING` filters after `GROUP BY` and accepts aggregates.
questions.explanation: `QUALIFY` is for window functions (A), and `SUM(1)` is still an aggregate (C).

questions.title: Off-by-One SUBSTR
questions.question: `product_code` values look like `XABCDE99`. An analyst needs characters 2 through 5 (`ABCD`) but writes `SUBSTR(product_code, 2, 5)` and gets `ABCDE`. What is the correct expression?
questions.shortAnswer: `SUBSTR(str, pos, len)` starts at a 1-based position and returns `len` characters. Starting at 2 with length 4 returns characters 2, 3, 4, and 5.
questions.explanation: The third argument is a length, not an end position, which is why length 5 returned one character too many. `LEFT(..., 5)` returns `XABCD` (B).

questions.title: Viewing a Query Plan
questions.question: Which statement shows the execution plan of a query without running it?
questions.shortAnswer: `EXPLAIN` returns the logical and physical plan of a statement. After a query runs, its query profile shows actual runtime metrics for each operator.
questions.explanation: `DESCRIBE` describes table schemas (B). Options C and D are not Databricks SQL statements.

questions.title: Above-Average Salaries
questions.question: Which query returns employees who earn more than the average salary?

choices.A: `SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)`

questions.shortAnswer: Aggregates cannot appear directly in `WHERE`. A scalar subquery computes the average once and compares each row to it.
questions.explanation: `MEAN` is a synonym for `AVG` in Databricks SQL, but it is still an aggregate, so option D fails for the same reason as option B.

questions.title: When the Result Cache Is Not Used
questions.question: Databricks SQL query result caches can return results without running the query again. In which case is a cached result NOT used?

choices.A: The query ran an hour ago on the same warehouse
choices.C: The underlying Delta table has been updated since the result was cached

questions.shortAnswer: Result caches are invalidated when the underlying tables are updated, so the query runs again against current data.
questions.explanation: The local result cache lives in a cluster's memory. The remote result cache (serverless only) is shared by all warehouses in a workspace. Both keep entries for up to 24 hours.

questions.title: What Photon Is  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: What is Photon?

choices.A: A BI tool for building dashboards
choices.B: A file format that replaces Parquet
choices.D: The Databricks-native vectorized query engine, which is the default engine for all SQL warehouses

questions.shortAnswer: Photon is the Databricks-native vectorized query engine. It speeds up SQL and DataFrame workloads, joins, aggregations, scans, and Delta and Parquet writes without code changes, and it is the default engine on every SQL warehouse.
questions.explanation: It is not a file format (B) or a scheduler (C).

questions.title: Photon and UDFs  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A query on a SQL warehouse calls a user-defined function (UDF). What happens to the parts of the query that Photon does not support?

choices.B: They fall back to the Spark runtime and the results stay correct

questions.shortAnswer: Photon does not support UDFs, RDD APIs, or Dataset APIs. Unsupported operations fall back to the standard Spark runtime, and results remain correct. Only that part of the query loses the Photon speed-up.
questions.explanation: Photon also gives little benefit to queries that already finish in under about two seconds.

questions.title: Did the Query Use Photon?  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: How can an analyst see how much of a query's work ran in Photon?

choices.C: Open the query profile; its execution details show the percentage of task time spent in Photon
choices.D: Look for the word "Photon" in the result set

questions.shortAnswer: The query profile's execution details show the share of task time spent in Photon. In the plan, Photon operators are shown in a different colour from standard Spark operators.
questions.explanation: `DESCRIBE HISTORY` lists table versions, not query execution (A).

questions.title: Spotting an Exploding Join  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A query that joins two tables returns hundreds of millions of rows and runs for a long time. Which tool shows where the row count explodes?

choices.D: The query profile, which shows rows, time, and memory for each operator

questions.shortAnswer: The query profile shows each operator with metrics such as time spent, rows, and peak memory. Databricks names exploding joins and full table scans as common mistakes it helps you find. Filter icons show the percentage of data pruned during scans.
questions.explanation: Where available, performance insights in the query details panel also suggest fixes, and **Optimize** opens Genie Code (formerly Databricks Assistant) to rewrite the query.

questions.title: Finding Failed Queries  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst needs every query that a colleague ran yesterday that failed. What is the fastest way?

choices.B: Open query history and filter by user, date range, and status
choices.C: Read the Delta transaction log of each table
choices.D: Ask a workspace admin to export the audit logs

questions.shortAnswer: Query history can be filtered by user, date range, compute, duration, query status, statement type, statement ID, and query tags.
questions.explanation: With serverless compute enabled, it also includes SQL and Python queries run on serverless compute for notebooks and jobs.

questions.title: Account-Wide Query Analysis  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A platform team wants to write SQL that finds the slowest queries across all warehouses in the account. Which source should they query?
questions.shortAnswer: The `system.query.history` system table holds query records across the account. By default, only admins can access system tables, so others need to be granted access.
questions.explanation: `information_schema.tables` lists table metadata (B), and `DESCRIBE HISTORY` covers one table's changes (C).

questions.title: Fast Result After a Restart  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: On a serverless SQL warehouse, an analyst runs a query, the warehouse stops and starts again, and the same query then returns instantly. No tables changed. Which cache explains this?

choices.A: The local result cache in the cluster's memory
choices.B: The disk cache on the cluster's SSDs
choices.C: The remote result cache, which persists across warehouse restarts and is shared by all warehouses in the workspace

questions.shortAnswer: The remote result cache is available only on serverless warehouses. It is a persistent cache shared by all warehouses in a workspace, it survives stops and restarts, and it keeps entries for 24 hours.
questions.explanation: The local result cache and the disk cache are cleared when the cluster stops (A, B). A query checks the local cache first, then the remote cache, and runs only when neither holds the result.

questions.title: Benchmarking Without the Cache  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst wants to time a query honestly and must stop Databricks SQL from returning a cached result. What should they run first?
questions.shortAnswer: `SET use_cached_result = false` turns off the result cache for the session. Databricks advises using it only for testing or benchmarking.
questions.explanation: `OPTIMIZE` rewrites data files and does not affect result caching (B).

questions.title: Who Deleted the Rows?  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: Rows disappeared from a Delta table overnight. Which command shows which operation ran, who ran it, and when?
questions.shortAnswer: `DESCRIBE HISTORY` returns each write to the table in reverse order, with the operation, user, timestamp, `operationParameters`, and `operationMetrics` (such as the number of deleted rows).
questions.explanation: `DESCRIBE DETAIL` shows current table metadata such as location and size (A). Option D reads the first version of the data but does not say who changed it.

questions.title: Rows Changed Between Versions  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst wants the rows that are in version 12 of the `orders` table but were not in version 10. Which query returns them?

choices.A: `SELECT * FROM orders VERSION AS OF 12 EXCEPT SELECT * FROM orders VERSION AS OF 10`
choices.C: `RESTORE TABLE orders TO VERSION AS OF 10`
choices.D: `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE version BETWEEN 10 AND 12`

questions.shortAnswer: Time travel can read two versions of the same table, and `EXCEPT` returns the rows of the first query that are missing from the second. This is a quick way to validate a load or compare results over time.
questions.explanation: `RESTORE` rolls the table back and changes it (C). Tables have no `version` column (D).

questions.title: Enabling Liquid Clustering  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: Which statement creates a table that uses liquid clustering on `customer_id`?
questions.shortAnswer: `CLUSTER BY` enables liquid clustering. For an existing table, use `ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (...)`. Databricks recommends liquid clustering for all new tables, including streaming tables and materialized views.
questions.explanation: Liquid clustering replaces partitioning and `ZORDER` and cannot be combined with them (A, B).

questions.title: Choosing Clustering Keys  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A 2 TB table is usually queried with `WHERE event_date = ...` and `WHERE country = ...`. Which columns should be the liquid clustering keys?

choices.A: The primary key column, whatever the queries filter on
choices.C: `event_date` and `country`, the columns most often used in filters

questions.shortAnswer: Choose clustering keys from the columns most often used in query filters. You can specify up to four keys.
questions.explanation: Clustering on columns that queries do not filter on does not help data skipping (A, D), and more than four keys is not allowed (B).

questions.title: Changing Clustering Keys  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst runs `ALTER TABLE sales CLUSTER BY (country)` on a table that already holds years of data. What happens to the existing data?

choices.A: The whole table is rewritten immediately during the `ALTER`
choices.B: The command fails because clustering keys cannot change
choices.C: The keys change without rewriting existing data; `OPTIMIZE` clusters data incrementally, and `OPTIMIZE ... FULL` reclusters all of it
choices.D: The table converts to a partitioned table

questions.shortAnswer: Liquid clustering keys can be redefined without rewriting existing data. `OPTIMIZE` is incremental and rewrites only what it needs. `OPTIMIZE table_name FULL` reclusters all records. Predictive optimization can run `OPTIMIZE` automatically on enabled tables.
questions.explanation: Keys can change at any time (B), and liquid clustering is not partitioning (D).

questions.title: Automatic Liquid Clustering  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: What does `CLUSTER BY AUTO` do, and what does it require?

choices.A: Databricks chooses the clustering keys based on how the table is queried; it requires a Unity Catalog managed table and predictive optimization
choices.B: It clusters by every column; it works on any table
choices.D: It partitions the table by date automatically

questions.shortAnswer: Automatic liquid clustering lets Databricks choose and change clustering keys to improve query performance. It works on Unity Catalog managed tables and needs predictive optimization for key selection and clustering, which run asynchronously.

questions.title: Missing Column in GROUP BY  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: `SELECT region, product, SUM(sales) FROM orders GROUP BY region` fails. Why?

choices.B: `product` is selected but is neither grouped nor aggregated

questions.shortAnswer: Every non-aggregated column in the `SELECT` list must appear in `GROUP BY`. Add `product` to `GROUP BY` (or use `GROUP BY ALL`), or remove it from the `SELECT` list.

questions.title: Comparing to NULL  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE discount = NULL` returns no rows, even though many orders have no discount. What is the fix?
questions.shortAnswer: Comparing anything to NULL with `=` returns NULL, not TRUE, so no rows pass the filter. Use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.
questions.explanation: Option C compares to the text `'NULL'`, which is a different value.

questions.title: LEFT JOIN That Behaves Like an INNER JOIN  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question:
An analyst wants every customer with their 2026 orders, including customers with no 2026 orders. The query is:

`SELECT c.id, o.amount FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_year = 2026`

Customers without 2026 orders are missing. What fixes it?

choices.D: Move the condition into the join: `ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.order_year = 2026`

questions.shortAnswer: For customers with no matching order, `o.order_year` is NULL, so the `WHERE` filter removes them and the outer join acts like an inner join. Filtering the right table in the `ON` clause keeps every customer.

questions.title: Where Genie's Answer Comes From  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A business user asks a Genie space, "How many orders shipped last month?" How does Genie produce the number?

choices.A: The model reads the table rows and counts them itself
choices.B: Genie generates a read-only SQL query that runs on the space's SQL warehouse, then summarises the result
choices.C: Genie looks the number up in a cache of previous dashboard results
choices.D: Genie exports the table to the model provider, which computes the answer

questions.shortAnswer: Genie translates the question into read-only SQL, runs it on the space's SQL warehouse, and returns the result table, a visualization, and a text summary.
questions.explanation: The model does not scan or count rows (A, D), and Genie does not answer from a dashboard cache (C). This is why Unity Catalog permissions apply: the generated SQL is executed like any other query.

questions.title: Warehouse Requirement  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst is creating a Genie space. Which SQL warehouse types can the space use?

choices.D: No warehouse — Genie uses its own compute

questions.shortAnswer: Genie requires a pro or serverless SQL warehouse; Databricks recommends serverless for performance.
questions.explanation: Classic warehouses are not supported (A). Serverless is recommended but not the only option (C). Generated SQL runs on the space's warehouse, not on separate Genie compute (D).

questions.title: PII and Genie  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A Genie space covers a `customers` table that has a column mask on `email` and a row filter that limits each sales rep to their own region. A sales rep asks Genie, "List the emails of all customers." What happens?

choices.A: Genie returns all emails because the space author created the space
choices.B: Genie refuses every question about the customers table
choices.C: The query runs under the rep's Unity Catalog permissions, so the mask and the row filter apply
choices.D: Genie returns all rows but hides the email column from the chart only

questions.shortAnswer: Genie runs on the author's warehouse, but data access is checked against the asking user's Unity Catalog permissions. Row filters and column masks apply per user.
questions.explanation: The author's identity does not widen access (A). Genie does not block the table (B), and masking is enforced by UC in the query result, not only in a chart (D).

questions.title: Consumer Permissions  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: The marketing team should be able to ask questions in a Genie space. Which combination is sufficient for a marketing user?

choices.A: `CAN USE` on the SQL warehouse and `CAN VIEW` on the space
choices.B: `CAN RUN` on the space and `SELECT` on every Unity Catalog object the space uses (plus consumer access or the Databricks SQL entitlement)

questions.shortAnswer: Consumers need at least `CAN VIEW` or `CAN RUN` on the space, `SELECT` on the underlying UC data, and the consumer-access or Databricks SQL entitlement.
questions.explanation: Consumers do **not** need warehouse permissions — queries run with the warehouse credentials the author embedded — so A adds an unnecessary grant and still misses data access. `CAN MANAGE` (C) and admin rights (D) are far more than needed and still don't grant data access by themselves.

questions.title: Trusted Assets  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: Which items are **trusted assets** in a Genie space?

choices.B: Parameterized example SQL queries and Unity Catalog SQL functions

questions.shortAnswer: Trusted assets are parameterized example queries and SQL functions whose exact logic an author verified; answers that use them come from that verified logic.
questions.explanation: Text instructions and synonyms (A) are context, not verified logic. Benchmarks (C) are only used to score accuracy. SQL expressions (D) are knowledge-store entries.

questions.title: Parameter Syntax  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An author wants an example query that answers "What is revenue for region X?" for any region. How is the parameter written in the example SQL?
questions.shortAnswer: Genie example queries use named parameters: type a colon followed by a name (`:parameter_name`), or click **Add parameter**.
questions.explanation: The gear icon sets the parameter's data type (String, Date, Date and Time, Decimal, Integer) and a comment. `?` placeholders, `{{ }}` mustache syntax, and `$` variables are not Genie's parameter syntax.

questions.title: Choosing a Curation Lever  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: Genie sometimes sums `paid_amount` and sometimes `invoice_total` when users ask about revenue. The business rule is that revenue is always `SUM(invoice_total)`. What is the recommended fix?

choices.A: Add a text instruction: "Revenue means invoice_total"
choices.B: Add a Measure SQL expression named `revenue` with code `SUM(invoice_total)` and synonyms such as "sales"
choices.C: Add a benchmark question about revenue
choices.D: Hide the `paid_amount` column from every user with a UC column mask

questions.shortAnswer: The curation guide says to prioritize SQL expressions and example SQL over text instructions, and to use text instructions only as a last resort. A Measure SQL expression encodes the KPI exactly.
questions.explanation: A text instruction (A) works less reliably. A benchmark (C) only measures accuracy — it does not change Genie's context. Masking a column (D) changes data access for everyone and is the wrong tool for an interpretation problem.

questions.title: Users Type Different Values  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: Users ask about "NYC", but the `city` column stores `New York City`. Genie keeps returning empty results. Which feature addresses this?

choices.A: Entity matching on the `city` column (in the column's Advanced settings)
choices.B: A text instruction listing every city alias

questions.shortAnswer: Entity matching (the value dictionary) maps what users type to the values actually stored. It works on string columns and requires format assistance; limits are 120 columns and 1,024 values per column.
questions.explanation: A long alias list in instructions (B) is the last-resort lever and hard to maintain. Warehouse size (C) does not affect interpretation. A row filter (D) restricts access, it doesn't resolve terms.

questions.title: Knowledge Store vs Unity Catalog  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A curator edits a table's description in the Genie space's knowledge store. What happens to the table comment in Unity Catalog?

choices.A: It is overwritten with the new description
choices.B: It is unchanged — the knowledge store is scoped to the space; **Reset** restores the UC description in the space
choices.D: It is copied into every other Genie space that uses the table

questions.shortAnswer: Knowledge-store descriptions and synonyms are scoped to the Genie space and do not overwrite metadata stored in Unity Catalog. **Reset** brings the UC description back into the space.
questions.explanation: To improve every space and tool at once, update the UC comment itself (for example with `COMMENT ON TABLE`).

questions.title: Benchmark Scoring  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A benchmark question has a SQL Answer that returns `region, revenue`. In a Chat-mode run, Genie returns the correct revenue per region plus an extra `order_count` column. How is the result labelled?

choices.A: Good, because the revenue values match
choices.B: Bad, because the result has extra columns
choices.D: It is skipped because the columns differ

questions.shortAnswer: Chat mode compares result sets with the SQL Answer. Results with extra columns are labelled **Bad**; exact matches, matches with different row sorting, or numeric values that round to the same 4 significant digits are **Good**.
questions.explanation: The curator can open the run, compare **Model output** with **Ground truth**, and relabel the result or use **Update ground truth**. Agent mode, by contrast, uses an LLM judge guided by the evaluation note.

questions.title: What Benchmarks Do  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: What is the purpose of benchmark questions in a Genie space?

choices.A: They are added to Genie's context so similar questions are answered better
choices.B: They score the space's accuracy systematically; they do not feed Genie's context
choices.D: They limit which questions users may ask

questions.shortAnswer: Benchmarks are test questions used only to evaluate accuracy. Up to 500 can be added, and each runs as a new conversation without threaded context.
questions.explanation: To improve answers, add example SQL, SQL expressions, functions, or instructions — benchmarks then confirm the improvement.

questions.title: Acting on User Feedback  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: After a month in production, users have marked several Genie answers with **Fix it** and **Request review**. What is the best maintenance workflow?

choices.A: Raise the warehouse size and ask users to retry
choices.B: Review the questions in the **Monitor** tab, curate fixes (instructions, trusted assets, knowledge store, or UC metadata), add the failing questions as benchmarks, and re-run benchmarks
choices.C: Delete the conversations so the feedback disappears

questions.shortAnswer: The exam's "optimize" skill is a loop: track user questions, accuracy, and feedback (Monitor tab, Weekly digest); update instructions and trusted assets from stakeholder input; refresh UC metadata; and validate with benchmarks.
questions.explanation: Bigger compute (A) does not fix interpretation errors, deleting conversations (C) throws away the evidence, and rebuilding (D) loses curation.

questions.title: Embedding a Space  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team wants the Genie space inside its intranet portal. What is required?

choices.A: Only a public link — anyone with the URL can use it without signing in
choices.B: A workspace admin adds the portal's domain to the allowed embedding surfaces, an author with `CAN MANAGE` copies the iframe code from **Share**, and end users still need space and data access
choices.C: Exporting the space as a static HTML file
choices.D: Granting the portal's web server `SELECT` on all tables

questions.shortAnswer: iframe embedding needs the host domain on the allowlist in Genie access-management settings, an author with at least `CAN MANAGE`, and end users with explicit access to the space and its data. Users who are not signed in are prompted to authenticate.
questions.explanation: There is no anonymous public access (A), no static export (C), and no grant to a web server (D).

questions.title: Scoping a Space  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst wants one Genie space for the whole company's 40 tables. What does the official curation guidance recommend?

choices.A: Add all 40 tables — the limit is 50
choices.B: Aim for five or fewer tables per space, prejoin tables into views or metric views when a topic needs more, and split broad domains into focused spaces
choices.C: Add the tables but hide every column except keys
choices.D: Use text instructions to describe all 40 tables

questions.shortAnswer: The curation guide says to aim for five or fewer tables and include only those needed for the questions the space should handle; the hard limit is 50 tables, views, or metric views.
questions.explanation: Many tables dilute Genie's context and make wrong joins more likely. Hiding columns (C) or long instructions (D) do not fix an over-broad scope.

questions.title: Hidden Columns  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A curator hides the `salary` column in a Genie space's knowledge store. Which statement is true?

choices.B: Genie no longer uses `salary` in its context, but users with direct table access can still query it — use UC grants or column masks to restrict access
choices.C: The column is dropped from the table
choices.D: Hiding the column also hides it in Catalog Explorer

questions.shortAnswer: Hiding a column only removes it from Genie's context. Hidden columns stay visible to users with direct table access, so hiding is not a security control.
questions.explanation: Restrict sensitive data with Unity Catalog permissions, row filters, and column masks.

questions.title: Connecting a BI Tool
questions.question: A team uses Tableau and wants to query tables through a Databricks SQL warehouse. Which connection method should they use?

choices.B: Direct access to the S3 bucket
choices.C: The JDBC or ODBC driver with the warehouse's connection details
choices.D: Polling a REST API every 5 minutes

questions.shortAnswer: BI tools connect to SQL warehouses through the Databricks JDBC and ODBC drivers. The connection uses the warehouse's server hostname and HTTP path plus an authentication method such as OAuth or a personal access token.
questions.explanation: Reading cloud storage directly bypasses Unity Catalog governance (B).

questions.title: Partner Connect
questions.question: A team wants to connect a partner ingestion tool such as Fivetran to the workspace without setting up compute and credentials by hand. Which feature helps?
questions.shortAnswer: Partner Connect connects the workspace to selected partner solutions from the Databricks UI. It provisions the Databricks resources the partner needs, such as a SQL warehouse, a service principal, and a personal access token.
questions.explanation: Partner Connect requires the Premium plan or above.

questions.title: Dropping Managed and External Tables
questions.question: An analyst drops a managed Delta table and then drops an external Delta table. What happens in each case?

choices.A: Both drops delete the data files and the metadata
choices.B: Both drops delete only the metadata
choices.C: Managed: the data and the metadata are deleted. External: only the metadata is deleted, and the files stay in storage
choices.D: External: the data and the metadata are deleted. Managed: only the metadata is deleted

questions.shortAnswer: Unity Catalog manages the storage of a managed table, so dropping the table also deletes its data. An external table only points at files you manage, so dropping it removes the table definition and leaves the files.
questions.explanation: This is why `SHOW TABLES` can stop listing a dropped external table while its files are still in cloud storage.

questions.title: Metastore vs Catalog
questions.question: In Unity Catalog, how are a metastore and a catalog related?

choices.A: The metastore is the top-level container for a region; catalogs are objects inside it
choices.B: They are two names for the same object
choices.D: Each workspace has its own metastore, and catalogs exist at the account level

questions.shortAnswer: A metastore is the top-level container of Unity Catalog metadata, created at the account level for each region. Workspaces in that region are attached to it, and it holds the catalogs, which hold schemas, which hold tables, views, volumes, and functions.

questions.title: External Table Files Deleted
questions.question: An external table points to `s3://company-data/raw/sales/`. A faulty pipeline deletes everything under that path. What happens when analysts query the table?

choices.A: The query fails, because the files the table points to no longer exist
choices.B: The table returns the last results from the cache forever
choices.C: Delta Lake restores the files from the transaction log automatically
choices.D: Unity Catalog drops the table automatically

questions.shortAnswer: An external table's data lives only at its storage path. Unity Catalog keeps the table definition, but once the files are gone there is nothing to read, so queries fail.
questions.explanation: The transaction log records changes but does not hold copies of the data, so it cannot recreate deleted files (C). Unity Catalog does not drop tables by itself (D).

questions.title: Which Component Does What?  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: Which platform component adds ACID transactions and time travel to data stored in cloud object storage?
questions.shortAnswer: Delta Lake is the open table format that adds ACID transactions, table history, and time travel on top of Parquet files in cloud storage.
questions.explanation: Unity Catalog governs access, lineage, and discovery (B). Lakeflow Jobs orchestrates tasks on a schedule or trigger (C). Databricks SQL provides SQL warehouses, the SQL editor, dashboards, and alerts (D).

questions.title: Delta Live Tables Today  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: The exam guide lists "Delta Live Tables" as a platform component. What is it called in the current documentation, and what does it do?

choices.B: Delta Sharing; it shares tables with partners
choices.D: Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines; you declare tables, materialized views, and streaming tables, and the pipeline manages dependencies, refreshes, and data quality

questions.shortAnswer: Delta Live Tables (DLT) became Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines, and on November 12, 2025 it was renamed Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines. The current docs also use the short form "Lakeflow pipelines". You declare what each dataset should contain, and the pipeline works out the order, refreshes, and expectations.
questions.explanation: On the exam, expect the older name. Lakeflow Jobs is the orchestrator (A).

questions.title: Orchestrating Tasks  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: A team wants to run a SQL query, then a notebook, then a pipeline refresh every night in that order, with retries and notifications. Which component should they use?
questions.shortAnswer: Lakeflow Jobs orchestrates tasks such as notebooks, SQL, pipelines, and Databricks SQL alerts, with schedules, dependencies, retries, and notifications.
questions.explanation: The other components store, govern, or share data. They do not schedule work.

questions.title: The Data Intelligence Engine  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: The exam guide names a "Data Intelligence Engine" as a platform component. What does it refer to?

choices.A: The query engine that replaces Spark
choices.B: A separate database for AI models
choices.C: The AI layer, which Databricks calls DatabricksIQ, that learns the semantics of an organisation's data and fuels the rest of the platform

questions.shortAnswer: When Databricks introduced the Data Intelligence Platform in November 2023, it described a Data Intelligence Engine called DatabricksIQ. It uses AI models to understand the semantics of enterprise data. For example, it generates descriptions and tags in Unity Catalog that make the whole platform aware of your jargon, acronyms, and metrics.
questions.explanation: Photon is the query engine (A), not the Data Intelligence Engine.

questions.title: What "Certified" Means  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: In Catalog Explorer, a table shows a certified badge (a check mark). What does that tell an analyst?

choices.A: The table has passed an automated data quality test
choices.B: The table has been flagged as a trusted, recommended asset with the `system.certification_status` tag set to `certified`

questions.shortAnswer: Certification is a system-governed tag, `system.certification_status`, with the values `certified` and `deprecated`. Certified assets show a check mark, and deprecated assets show a restricted icon, so users can tell trusted data from data they should stop using.
questions.explanation: The badge is a governance label. It does not run tests, encrypt data, or change permissions.

questions.title: Viewing Lineage  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst opens a table in Catalog Explorer and wants an interactive diagram of its upstream sources and downstream consumers. What should they do, and what privilege do they need?

choices.A: Open the History tab; MODIFY on the table
choices.B: Run `DESCRIBE HISTORY`; ownership of the table
choices.C: Open the Lineage tab and click **See Lineage Graph**; at least BROWSE on the table's parent catalog
choices.D: Open the Permissions tab; MANAGE on the table

questions.shortAnswer: The Lineage tab lists related tables, notebooks, jobs, and dashboards, and **See Lineage Graph** opens the interactive graph. Viewing lineage requires at least the BROWSE privilege on the parent catalog. Seeing notebooks, jobs, or dashboards in the graph also requires workspace permissions on them.
questions.explanation: `DESCRIBE HISTORY` shows table versions, not lineage (B).

questions.title: Role of Databricks Marketplace  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: What is Databricks Marketplace?

choices.A: A store for buying more DBUs
choices.D: An open exchange where providers publish data products such as datasets, AI models, notebooks, and apps that consumers can access from their workspace

questions.shortAnswer: Marketplace is an open exchange for data and AI products. Listings can be free or commercial, and public or private. Some are available as soon as you request them and accept the terms, while others need the provider's approval.
questions.explanation: Marketplace uses Delta Sharing (renamed OpenSharing on June 10, 2026) for secure exchange, so the data is not copied into your workspace.

questions.title: Getting Marketplace Data  *(2025 blueprint)*
questions.question: An analyst finds a free dataset in Databricks Marketplace that is available instantly. How do they start querying it?

choices.A: Download CSV files and upload them through the UI
choices.B: Ask the provider to email credentials for their database
choices.C: Request access from Marketplace in their Databricks workspace; the dataset is then available as a catalog they can query
choices.D: Run `COPY INTO` from the provider's bucket

questions.shortAnswer: Requesting data products needs a Databricks workspace. Datasets are usually delivered as catalogs of tabular data, shared live with OpenSharing (formerly Delta Sharing), so there is no ingestion pipeline to build.
questions.explanation: Browsing the public Marketplace does not require a workspace, but getting the data does.

questions.title: Appending a New Column
questions.question: An analyst appends data that has an extra column to an existing Delta table with `df.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("sales")`. The new column is not in the table schema. What happens?

choices.A: The column is added to the table schema automatically
choices.B: The write fails, because Delta Lake enforces the table schema unless schema evolution is enabled
choices.C: The new column is dropped silently
choices.D: The column is stored as a JSON string

questions.shortAnswer: Delta Lake enforces the schema on write. To add the new column during the write, enable schema evolution, for example with `.option("mergeSchema", "true")`.
questions.explanation: Delta never drops or reshapes columns silently (C, D).

questions.title: Replacing a Schema
questions.question: What does the `overwriteSchema` option do when it is combined with `mode("overwrite")` in a Delta Lake write?

choices.A: Replaces the table's schema with the schema of the data being written
choices.B: Adds new columns to the existing schema
choices.C: Checks that the schemas match and fails if they differ
